result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.get_degree_distribution()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Get degree distribution as a mapping from degree to count. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L32580-L32637){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.get_degree_distribution() ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Degree distribution](/assets/graphs/get-degree-distribution.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="A five-node graph with each node's degree in a badge, and a bar chart of how many nodes have each degree: one node of degree 1, one of degree 2, and three of degree 3." width="100%"} Returns a histogram of node degrees, showing how many nodes have each degree value. Useful for analyzing network topology and identifying hub nodes or scale-free properties. Each node is counted once, under its degree. Only degree values that occur appear as keys, so there are no zero-count entries, and the counts add up to the number of nodes. The distribution is a compact fingerprint of a network's structure: - a long tail of rare, very high degrees points to hubs and a possibly scale-free network - a narrow peak around one value suggests a regular or random-like network - a large count at degree `0` or `1` reveals many isolated or peripheral nodes In undirected graphs the degrees match `get_degree()` (parallel edges each count and a self-loop counts twice). In directed graphs, each node is binned by its total degree (in-degree plus out-degree), also matching `get_degree()`. Edge weights are ignored. The dictionary is not ordered by degree; wrap it in `sorted()` to read it in order. An empty graph gives an empty dictionary. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [dict[int, int]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Dictionary mapping degree values to the number of nodes with that degree. ::: ## See Also {.doc-see-also} [](`~degrees`) : Each node's degree, rather than counts per degree. [](`~get_average_degree`) : The mean degree as a single number. ## Examples {.doc-examples} Four spokes each have degree `1`, while the hub alone has degree `4`: ::: {#3520f9b8 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ( ec.Graph() .add_nodes(["Hub", "A", "B", "C", "D"]) .add_edges([("Hub", "A"), ("Hub", "B"), ("Hub", "C"), ("Hub", "D")]) ) graph.get_degree_distribution() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` {1: 4, 4: 1} ``` ::: ::: On a real social network the distribution is skewed: in Zachary's karate club most members have only a few ties, while a handful of central members have 10 or more. Sorting by degree makes the tail easy to see: ::: {#f3247e65 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} dict(sorted(ec.karate_club().get_degree_distribution().items())) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` {1: 1, 2: 11, 3: 6, 4: 6, 5: 3, 6: 2, 9: 1, 10: 1, 12: 1, 16: 1, 17: 1} ``` ::: :::
